title: Unsolved mysteries of the Bayeux Tapestry - hidden penis to missing ending
excerpt: The Daily Star's Ed went to see the famous work and now he takes you through the five best hidden moments and unsolved mysteries inside the iconic thousand-year-old artefact
content:
Be it horse-riding Normans heading to the Battle of Hastings, or King Harold desperately clutching an arrow lodged in his eye, the Bayeux Tapestry features numerous iconic moments in the classic story of 1066.

And yet, despite every inch of the 68.3m tapestry being meticulously studied by historians for centuries, the legendary piece still contains a number of parts that baffle experts today.

From hidden genitalia and mystery dwarfs to the artwork’s lost ending, here are five secrets of the Bayeux Tapestry to keep an eye out for when you visit.

Willy or Willy not?

It may sound like a bit of a childish debate, but history buffs have spent years analysing the various genitalia featured on the Tapestry, with a controversial “94th penis” at the centre of a row dating back all the way back to, er, 2025.

‌

While respected Oxford historian Professor George Garnett is adamant that there are 93 penises in the embroidery, with 88 belonging to horses and the other five dangling off some of the Tapestry’s many naked blokes, a secret hidden appendage has been theorised by several other experts.

Dr Christopher Monk, who specialises in sexuality and nudity in early medieval culture, points to a large, protruding sausage-shaped object hanging out of one soldier’s tunic, arguing that its shape, position and flesh-like colour point to it being a penis, as opposed to a scabbard for his sword as previously believed.

11th-century Fleabag

Much like the TV show Fleabag, the Bayeux Tapestry features a mysterious woman who may or may not have got down and dirty with a mysterious and somewhat slutty priest.

‌

Labelled on the Tapestry as Ælfgyva, scholars have put forward a number of theories as to who the unknown lady might be, including Emma of Normandy, William the Conqueror’s great-aunt.

She is depicted having her face caressed by an unknown priest, who appears in the border below to also be shown fully naked and displaying a not-so-subtle erect penis.

Boffins have suggested the shocking scene may have been intended to undermine William’s claim to the throne, or could simply be a reference to a now-lost bit of gossip that would have amused viewers back in the 11th century.

‌

Dwarf star

One of the more mysterious figures depicted in the Tapestry is Turold, a mischievous-looking dwarf who appears to be swinging from the reins of a horse.

While little is known about the real figure, the name Turold is used in texts from the time to refer to storytellers, prompting some historians to suggest that the cheeky-looking lad may actually be the Tapestry’s chief creator.

While we are certainly convinced by this theory, others have suggested that the name “Turold” may refer to the nobleman standing next to the horse, meaning the mysterious dwarf’s true identity may be lost forever.

‌

Eye think not…

Probably the Bayeux Tapestry’s most famous scene is the moment when King Harold gets shot in the eye by an arrow, helping William secure his victory at the Battle of Hastings.

However, many historians believe the iconic arrow itself may have been added centuries later by naughty 19th-century restorers looking to put their own spin on the story.

Experts have analysed the stitching around Harold’s eye and found that the golden arrow was almost certainly added during restoration in the 1800s, although they believe some form of projectile was originally stitched there too.

‌

And in what is basically a super-nerdy version of Cluedo, some academics have argued that the original weapon may have been a spear.

Missing ending

While almost all of the surviving 68.3m tapestry remains in remarkably good nick, the final parts of the work have disappeared, with historians having no clue what might have happened to them.

While most agree that the final moments probably showed the victorious William the Conqueror’s coronation in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, what really fascinates those who study the Tapestry is why the ending scene disappeared, and whether this was due to a deliberate conspiracy as opposed to some medieval mishap.

‌

It has been suggested that a possible act of sabotage may have been committed in order to undermine the Norman king’s claim to the throne, although exactly who would have committed this Just Stop Oil-esque protest is not known.
